topic: Identification of ions by chemical and spectroscopic means (chemistry only)
subject: chemistry

items.q: A student holds a small sample of an unknown ionic compound on a clean wire in a hot Bunsen flame, and a strong colour appears. What does the flame colour identify?
items.correct: the metal ion, the cation, present in that compound
items.misconception: the negative ion, the anion, in the compound
items.why: Compound names end with the negative ion, so students read the last word of the name as the thing being tested. Flame tests identify metal ions (cations). Negative ions are found with the carbonate, halide and sulfate tests.
items.random_wrong: the compound as a whole and not one of its ions

items.q: Lithium chloride is held on a clean wire in a hot Bunsen flame. What is seen?
items.correct: The flame turns a deep crimson colour.
items.misconception: The flame turns a bright yellow colour.
items.why: Sodium street lamps and burning sodium both look orange, and orange-red sits in the same list of colours for calcium. The specification is exact: sodium compounds result in a yellow flame. Orange-red belongs to calcium.
items.random_wrong: The flame turns an orange-red colour.

items.q: Sodium chloride is used in a flame test. Which statement describes the result?
items.correct: Sodium ions colour the flame yellow.
items.misconception: Sodium ions colour the flame bright orange.
items.why: Sodium street lamps and burning sodium both look orange, and orange-red sits in the same list of colours for calcium. The specification is exact: sodium compounds result in a yellow flame. Orange-red belongs to calcium.
items.random_wrong: Sodium ions colour the flame crimson red.

items.q: Potassium bromide is tested in a flame test. What is the result?
items.correct: The flame colour produced is lilac.
items.misconception: The flame colour produced is yellow.
items.why: Lilac is an unfamiliar colour word, so students replace it with a colour they already use for another metal in the list. Potassium compounds result in a lilac flame. Yellow belongs to sodium, crimson to lithium and orange-red to calcium.
items.random_wrong: The flame colour produced is crimson.

items.q: Calcium nitrate gives a distinctive colour in a flame test. Which colour is it?
items.correct: an orange-red flame colour
items.misconception: a bright crimson colour
items.why: Crimson and orange-red are both reds, and lithium and calcium are learned together as the two 'red' flame colours. Lithium is crimson; calcium is orange-red. The two must be kept apart.
items.random_wrong: a pale green flame colour

items.q: Copper(II) sulfate is held in a hot Bunsen flame during a flame test. What is seen?
items.correct: The flame is coloured a bright green.
items.misconception: The flame is coloured a crimson red.
items.why: Crimson and orange-red are both reds, and lithium and calcium are learned together as the two 'red' flame colours. Lithium is crimson; calcium is orange-red. The two must be kept apart.
items.random_wrong: The flame is coloured pale blue.

items.q: A solution contains both sodium ions and potassium ions. In a flame test only a yellow colour is seen. Why is the lilac colour of potassium not seen?
items.correct: The intense sodium colour masks the lilac.
items.misconception: The potassium ions are destroyed in the flame.
items.why: Not seeing something is read as it no longer being there, rather than as it being hidden. Both ions are still present. If a sample containing a mixture of ions is used, some flame colours can be masked.
items.random_wrong: The two colours mix to give a new colour.

items.q: An unknown compound gives a yellow flame test colour. Its solution gives a white precipitate when dilute hydrochloric acid and then barium chloride solution are added. What is the compound?
items.correct: sodium sulfate
items.misconception: sodium carbonate
items.why: The carbonate test is the first test met that uses a dilute acid, so the acid rather than the fizzing becomes the cue for carbonate. Carbonates are shown by fizzing that gives carbon dioxide. Dilute acid is also used in the halide and sulfate tests, where a precipitate, not a carbonate, is the result.
items.random_wrong: potassium sulfate

items.q: Sodium hydroxide solution is added to a solution of an unknown salt and a precipitate forms. Which ion in the salt does this test identify?
items.correct: the positive metal ion in the salt, its cation
items.misconception: the negative ion in the salt, its anion
items.why: A precipitate needs both ions, so students credit the wrong half of the salt with the result. Sodium hydroxide solution can be used to identify some metal ions (cations); the precipitate is the metal hydroxide.
items.random_wrong: the sodium ion in the sodium hydroxide

items.q: Sodium hydroxide solution is added, a few drops at a time, to separate solutions of aluminium ions, calcium ions and magnesium ions. What is seen in each tube?
items.correct: A white precipitate forms in all three tubes.
items.misconception: A white precipitate forms in two of the tubes.
items.why: Because the precipitate dissolves again in excess, students remember only the clear final solution. A white precipitate forms first; it dissolves only when excess sodium hydroxide solution is added.
items.random_wrong: A coloured precipitate forms in each tube.

items.q: Excess sodium hydroxide solution is now added to the three white precipitates formed from aluminium, calcium and magnesium ions. What happens?
items.correct: Only the aluminium hydroxide dissolves.
items.misconception: Only the calcium hydroxide dissolves.
items.why: Calcium hydroxide is met as limewater, a solution, so students assume it is the soluble one. The precipitate that redissolves in excess sodium hydroxide solution is aluminium hydroxide.
items.random_wrong: All three of the white hydroxides dissolve.

items.q: Which set of metal ions all give coloured precipitates when sodium hydroxide solution is added to their solutions?
items.correct: copper(II), iron(II) and iron(III)
items.misconception: aluminium, calcium and magnesium ions
items.why: The two sets of three ions are learned as one list and are easily swapped. Aluminium, calcium and magnesium give white precipitates; copper(II), iron(II) and iron(III) give coloured ones.
items.random_wrong: copper(II), calcium and magnesium ions

items.q: Sodium hydroxide solution is added to iron(III) chloride solution. What is seen?
items.correct: a brown precipitate is seen
items.misconception: a green precipitate forms
items.why: The two iron ions differ only by a Roman numeral, so the pairing of colour to charge is easily reversed. Iron(II) forms a green precipitate; iron(III) forms a brown precipitate.
items.random_wrong: a blue precipitate forms

items.q: A solution gives a green precipitate when sodium hydroxide solution is added. Which ion does the solution contain?
items.correct: The solution contains iron(II) ions.
items.misconception: The solution contains copper(II) ions.
items.why: Copper is linked to green from the flame test and from green copper roofs, so green is carried across. Copper(II) forms a blue precipitate with sodium hydroxide solution; the green flame is a separate result.
items.random_wrong: It is a solution of iron(III) ions.

items.q: Sodium hydroxide solution is added to copper(II) sulfate solution and a blue precipitate forms. Which equation for this reaction is correct and balanced?
items.correct: CuSO4 + 2NaOH -> Cu(OH)2 + Na2SO4
items.misconception: CuSO4 + NaOH -> Cu(OH)2 + Na2SO4
items.why: Students copy the reactants across without counting atoms, and the equation looks tidy. A 2+ metal ion needs two hydroxide ions: CuSO4 + 2NaOH -> Cu(OH)2 + Na2SO4 is the balanced equation.
items.random_wrong: CuSO4 + 2NaOH -> Cu(OH)2 + 2Na2SO4

items.q: Iron(II) sulfate solution reacts with sodium hydroxide solution to give a green precipitate. Which equation is correct and balanced?
items.correct: FeSO4 + 2NaOH -> Fe(OH)2 + Na2SO4
items.misconception: Fe2SO4 + 3NaOH -> Fe(OH)3 + Na2SO4
items.why: Iron(III) compounds are met more often, so the 3+ charge is treated as iron's only charge. Iron(II) forms Fe(OH)2 and iron(III) forms Fe(OH)3; the Roman numeral gives the charge.
items.random_wrong: 2FeSO4 + 4NaOH -> 2Fe(OH)2 + Na2SO4

items.q: Dilute hydrochloric acid is added to a white solid that is thought to be a carbonate. What is seen, and what gas is given off?
items.correct: It fizzes, giving off carbon dioxide gas.
items.misconception: It fizzes, giving off hydrogen gas.
items.why: Acid plus metal gives hydrogen, and that far more common reaction is applied to carbonates too. Carbonates react with dilute acids to form carbon dioxide gas.
items.random_wrong: It fizzes, giving off oxygen gas.

items.q: The gas given off when a carbonate reacts with a dilute acid is bubbled through limewater. What is the positive result?
items.correct: The limewater turns cloudy, or milky.
items.misconception: The limewater relights a glowing splint.
items.why: The gas tests are learned as a set and the splint tests are swapped between gases. Oxygen relights a glowing splint. Carbon dioxide is identified with limewater, which turns cloudy.
items.random_wrong: The limewater turns a bright blue.

items.q: Dilute nitric acid and then silver nitrate solution are added to a solution of an unknown halide. A cream precipitate forms. What does the solution contain?
items.correct: The unknown solution contains bromide ions.
items.misconception: The unknown solution contains chloride ions.
items.why: White and cream are hard to tell apart, so the pairing with the halide is easily reversed. Silver chloride is white, silver bromide is cream and silver iodide is yellow.
items.random_wrong: The unknown solution contains carbonate ions.

items.q: A solution is acidified with dilute nitric acid and silver nitrate solution is added. A yellow precipitate forms. Which ion is present?
items.correct: the iodide ion, I-
items.misconception: the bromide ion, Br-
items.why: White and cream are hard to tell apart, so the pairing with the halide is easily reversed. Silver chloride is white, silver bromide is cream and silver iodide is yellow.
items.random_wrong: the chloride ion, Cl-

items.q: A student wants to show that a solution contains sulfate ions. What should be added, and what is a positive result?
items.correct: dilute hydrochloric acid, then barium chloride solution: a white precipitate
items.misconception: dilute nitric acid, then silver nitrate solution: a white precipitate
items.why: The halide test and the sulfate test both use an acid and then a solution, and both can give a white precipitate. Sulfate ions produce a white precipitate with barium chloride solution in the presence of dilute hydrochloric acid.
items.random_wrong: dilute hydrochloric acid, then sodium hydroxide: a white precipitate

items.q: Barium chloride solution is added to a solution in the presence of dilute hydrochloric acid, and a white precipitate forms. What does this show?
items.correct: Sulfate ions are present in the solution.
items.misconception: Chloride ions are present in this solution.
items.why: The word chloride appears in the reagent's name, so it is read as the ion being detected. The reagent supplies barium ions; the white precipitate is barium sulfate, so sulfate ions are present.
items.random_wrong: Carbonate ions are present in solution.

items.q: In Required practical 7 a student is given a solution of a single unknown ionic compound and must name it. Which plan will identify the compound?
items.correct: a flame test, then a test for the anion
items.misconception: adding sodium hydroxide, then more of it
items.why: A precipitate needs both ions, so students credit the wrong half of the salt with the result. Sodium hydroxide solution can be used to identify some metal ions (cations); the precipitate is the metal hydroxide.
items.random_wrong: adding barium chloride solution on its own

items.q: The specification describes instrumental methods of analysis. Which three words does it use?
items.correct: accurate, sensitive and rapid
items.misconception: accurate and sensitive, but slow
items.why: Machines in industry are pictured as needing long, careful runs, and accuracy is assumed to cost time. The specification states that instrumental methods are accurate, sensitive and rapid.
items.random_wrong: cheap, simple and easy to carry

items.q: Give one advantage of using an instrumental method instead of the chemical tests in this specification.
items.correct: It can detect a very small amount of a substance quickly.
items.misconception: It can be used without taking a sample at all.
items.why: Sensitive is read as needing no sample at all, rather than needing only a very small one. A sample is still needed; the advantage is that a very small sample is enough.
items.random_wrong: It gives a result that never needs any checking.

items.q: Flame emission spectroscopy is an instrumental method. What is it used to analyse?
items.correct: the metal ions present in solutions
items.misconception: the non-metal ions present in solids
items.why: Students want a single instrument that replaces every chemical test in the section. Flame emission spectroscopy is used to analyse metal ions in solutions.
items.random_wrong: the gases given off by a solution

items.q: In flame emission spectroscopy the sample is put into a flame. What happens to the light given out, and what is the output?
items.correct: It passes into a spectroscope, giving a line spectrum.
items.misconception: It is absorbed by the sample, giving a set of dark bands.
items.why: Flame tests are judged by eye, so the instrument is imagined as a better way of seeing one colour. The light given out is passed through a spectroscope, and the output is a line spectrum.
items.random_wrong: It passes through a coloured filter, giving one colour.

items.q: A student is given the line spectrum of a solution together with a reference set of line spectra for known metal ions. The sample spectrum contains every line of the lithium reference and every line of the calcium reference. What should the student conclude?
items.correct: Lithium ions and calcium ions are both present.
items.misconception: Only the ion with the brighter lines is present.
items.why: Flame tests give one visible colour, so students expect one answer from a spectrum too. A line spectrum can show several metal ions at once; each set of lines matching a reference means that ion is present.
items.random_wrong: A new metal ion not in the reference set is there.

items.q: Sodium hydroxide solution is added to iron(III) chloride solution and a brown precipitate forms. Which equation is correct and balanced?
items.correct: FeCl3 + 3NaOH -> Fe(OH)3 + 3NaCl
items.misconception: FeCl3 + 2NaOH -> Fe(OH)2 + 2NaCl
items.why: Cu(OH)2 and Fe(OH)2 are the worked examples met first, so the 2:1 ratio is copied to every metal ion without checking its charge. The number of hydroxide ions matches the charge on the metal ion: iron(III) gives Fe(OH)3 and needs 3NaOH.
items.random_wrong: FeCl3 + 3NaOH -> Fe(OH)3 + NaCl3

items.q: A solution is analysed by flame emission spectroscopy. Sample lines (nm): 589, 671. Reference lines (nm): sodium 589; lithium 671; potassium 766; calcium 622. Which metal ions does the sample contain?
items.correct: lithium and sodium ions
items.misconception: sodium ions on their own
items.why: Flame tests give one visible colour, so students expect one answer from a spectrum too. A line spectrum can show several metal ions at once; each set of lines matching a reference means that ion is present.
items.random_wrong: sodium and potassium ions

items.q: What colour flame do calcium compounds give?
items.correct: Calcium compounds result in an orange-red flame.
items.misconception: Calcium gives a yellow flame.
items.why: Orange and yellow look similar in a Bunsen flame, and the sodium yellow is the colour students remember best. Calcium is orange-red; yellow belongs to sodium.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: What colour flame do copper compounds give?
items.correct: Copper compounds result in a green flame.
items.misconception: Copper gives a blue flame.
items.why: Copper(II) sulfate solution is blue and copper(II) hydroxide is a blue precipitate, so blue is strongly linked to copper. In a flame test copper compounds result in a green flame. Blue is the colour of the copper(II) hydroxide precipitate, not the flame.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: What does a flame colour identify?
items.correct: The metal ion, the cation, in the compound.
items.misconception: The colour is a property of the whole compound, not of one ion.
items.why: Students think in substances rather than ions, so 'copper sulfate burns green' feels like a fact about the compound. All copper compounds give the same green flame, whatever the negative ion, because the colour comes from the metal ion alone.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: What is seen when two metal ions are present?
items.correct: The stronger colour is seen; the other can be masked.
items.misconception: The two colours mix to give a completely new, third colour.
items.why: Mixing paints or coloured lights gives a new colour, so the same is expected of flame colours. Flame colours are not mixed like paint; one intense colour simply hides the other.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Which white precipitate dissolves in excess sodium hydroxide?
items.correct: Only aluminium hydroxide dissolves.
items.misconception: All three white precipitates dissolve if enough sodium hydroxide is added.
items.why: Students generalise 'excess dissolves the precipitate' from the aluminium case to every white precipitate. Only the aluminium hydroxide precipitate dissolves in excess sodium hydroxide solution; calcium and magnesium hydroxides stay.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: What gas do carbonates give with dilute acids?
items.correct: Carbon dioxide.
items.misconception: Carbonates give off oxygen because the carbonate ion contains oxygen.
items.why: Counting the oxygen atoms in the formula is mistaken for predicting the product. The gas formed is carbon dioxide, identified because it turns limewater cloudy.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: What does limewater do in a positive test?
items.correct: It turns cloudy, or milky.
items.misconception: Limewater turns blue when carbon dioxide is bubbled through.
items.why: Colour-change indicators are the commonest test students meet, so a colour rather than a cloudiness is expected. Carbon dioxide turns limewater cloudy; the cloudiness is solid calcium carbonate.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: What colour is silver iodide?
items.correct: Yellow.
items.misconception: Silver iodide is white, like the other silver halides.
items.why: Iodine solution is brown, so no colour is firmly attached to iodide and white is used as a default. Silver iodide is yellow.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Which acid is used in the test for halide ions?
items.correct: Dilute nitric acid.
items.misconception: Dilute hydrochloric acid is used before adding silver nitrate.
items.why: Hydrochloric acid is the acid used most often in the laboratory, and it is the acid used in the sulfate test. Halide ions produce precipitates with silver nitrate solution in the presence of dilute nitric acid. Hydrochloric acid would add chloride ions of its own.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: What else can a line spectrum give?
items.correct: The concentration of the metal ions.
items.misconception: A line spectrum can only say which ions are present, never how much.
items.why: Identification is the obvious use, so the quantitative use is overlooked. The line spectrum can be analysed to identify the metal ions in the solution and to measure their concentrations.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: How is an unknown single ionic compound identified?
items.correct: One test for the metal ion and one for the negative ion.
items.misconception: A flame test on its own is enough to name the compound.
items.why: The flame test is quick and gives a clear result, so it feels like a complete identification. The flame test names only the metal ion; a second test is needed for the negative ion before the compound can be named.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Are instrumental methods cheaper than chemical tests?
items.correct: No; the instrument is expensive to buy and to run.
items.misconception: An instrumental method must be cheaper because a machine does the work.
items.why: Automatic is equated with cheap, and the cost of buying and maintaining the instrument is invisible to a student. The advantages stated are accuracy, sensitivity and speed. Instruments are costly, so a simple chemical test can be the cheaper option.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

specSource: AQA GCSE Chemistry (8462) specification; section 4.8.3 Identification of ions by chemical and spectroscopic means (chemistry only)
